transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it's nice to meet you too. I, uh, I guess what brings me in is just... I cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. Not for the life of me. It's getting so bad at work, and I've been a carpenter for, gosh, almost forty years now, so you'd think I'd have a handle on things, right? But lately, it's just impossible. I'll be right in the middle of measuring out a cut, or trying to review an invoice in the trailer, and the second something else happens—like, if someone starts up a table saw on the other side of the site, or even if one of the guys just walks past the window—bam. My focus is gone. I'm looking at them, wondering what they're working on, or I'll suddenly remember this completely different job we're supposed to bid on next week, and I'll start thinking about the lumber costs for that. And then, before I know it, twenty minutes have gone by, I haven't made my cut, I haven't finished the invoice, and I'm off doing something else entirely. It's like the whole day just completely gets away from me, piece by piece, and I get to the end of my shift and realize I've barely finished a single thing I set out to do in the morning. It's just exhausting, you know? I didn't used to be this scattered.
Did this trouble focusing start only recently?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've been thinking about the timeline a lot lately, just trying to make sense of it all. I mean, I've always been a little distractible, sure, but nothing like this. This... this specific level of trouble, where I feel like my brain is just a sieve, that's been going on for about a year and a month now. I know the exact timing because it all started right after I broke my wrist. It was a stupid accident, really—just slipped on some ice loading up the truck—but it meant I couldn't swing a hammer or handle the heavy materials for a good long while. So, the boss, he's a good guy, he shifted me into the shop, doing all the paperwork, the ordering, the invoicing, and just sort of supervising the younger guys instead of doing the hands-on carpentry I've been doing my whole life. 

And I thought, okay, this'll be fine, it's a nice break for my body, right? But sitting at that desk... oh my gosh. When I'm working with my hands, building something, it's like my body keeps my brain anchored. But sitting there looking at spreadsheets and supplier emails? It's like my mind just detaches and floats away. I'll be trying to reconcile a lumber bill, and then I'll hear the guys laughing outside, and suddenly I'm out there in my head, or I'm reorganizing the filing cabinet, or I'm just staring at the screen thinking about a completely different project. So, yeah, it's been about thirteen months of this absolute chaos since they moved me off the tools and into the office. It's just been a completely different world, and honestly, I don't think my brain was built for it.
Did you hit your head when you fell on the ice?

No, no, I didn't hit my head. I know that's probably what you're thinking, like maybe I got a concussion or something, right? Because I know that can mess with your memory and your focus. My brother-in-law got a bad concussion a few years back playing softball, of all things, and he was in a fog for months. But no, nothing like that for me. 

When I slipped, it was one of those really sudden things where your feet just go completely out from under you. You know how black ice is, you don't even see it until you're already going down. I was carrying this heavy bundle of trim, and I think my instinct was just to drop it and put my hand out to catch myself, which, you know, they always tell you not to do, but it's just a reflex! So all my weight, plus the momentum, just went right into my right wrist. Heard a horrible crunching sound, which I'll never forget. But my head? No, my head never touched the ground. I ended up kind of twisting as I fell, so I landed hard on my side and my arm, but my head was perfectly safe. 

I even went to the emergency room right after—well, one of the guys drove me, I obviously couldn't drive with my wrist swelling up like a balloon—and they checked me over pretty thoroughly. Did the x-rays on the arm, obviously, but the doctor there, he asked me the same thing, if I hit my head, if I felt dizzy or sick, and I told him no. And I haven't had any headaches or anything since then, either. Just the wrist. And then, of course, the whole nightmare of being stuck at that desk trying to do paperwork when my brain just absolutely refuses to cooperate. So, yeah, no head injury, just a really, really busted wrist and a whole lot of frustration.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?

Down? Depressed? No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, frustrated? Absolutely. I am so frustrated I could spit nails most days, just because I can't seem to get my brain to do what it's supposed to do. But depressed... no. It's not like a sadness or a dark cloud or anything like that. I know what that looks like. My older sister went through a really rough patch with depression a few years back, and she couldn't even bring herself to get out of bed or make a cup of tea. It was just heartbreaking to watch her go through that. 

But for me, it's nothing like that. I still have plenty of energy. I'm up at 5:00 AM every morning, bright and early, I make my coffee, I pack my lunch, I'm ready to tackle the day. I still love my life, you know? I love my husband, I love spending time with my grandkids on the weekends—we just built a little birdhouse together last Sunday, actually, which was wonderful because I finally got to use my hands again and just show them how to sand down the edges properly. So the joy is still there, and the motivation to do things is definitely still there. 

It's just... it's just this invisible wall I hit the second I sit down at that desk in the trailer. It's exasperating, and sure, I come home complaining about it to my husband, probably talking his ear off about how I stared at a purchase order for an hour without reading a single word. He's even asked me a couple of times, "Honey, are you getting depressed about being off the tools?" And I tell him the exact same thing I'm telling you: I'm not sad, and I'm not down in the dumps. I'm just completely and utterly fed up with my own brain for not cooperating with this office work. So, no, definitely not depressed. Just... annoyed. Very, very annoyed with myself.
As a child in school, did you often have trouble paying attention?

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask about school, because I was actually just talking to my husband about this the other day when we were cleaning out the attic and found some of my old report cards. My mom kept everything, bless her heart, every single little piece of paper. And looking back at those... oh boy. Even way back then, like, grade school, definitely before I was even twelve years old, it was the same story over and over. 

I mean, I wasn't a bad kid. I wasn't running around the classroom causing trouble or anything like that. But every single teacher, from Mrs. Higgins in second grade to Mr. Abernathy in fifth, they all wrote the exact same things in the margins. "Bright but careless." That was the phrase. "She’s a bright girl, but she’s so careless." 

I was always, always losing my homework. I’d do it at the kitchen table, I know I did it, but by the time I got to school, it was just... gone. Vanished. Or the teacher would stand at the front of the room and give us three simple instructions, like, "Get out your math book, turn to page forty, and do the odd numbers." And by the time she finished the sentence, I was already lost. I’d have my spelling book out and be wondering what we were having for lunch. 

I spent half my childhood just staring out the window. I remember in fourth grade, my desk was right next to this big window that looked out over the playground and the street, and I would just watch the cars go by, or watch the janitor sweeping the sidewalk, instead of finishing whatever worksheet we were supposed to be doing. My mom would get so frustrated at parent-teacher conferences, because they’d tell her I just wasn't applying myself. But it wasn't that I didn't want to! It was just like my brain had a mind of its own, even back then. So, yeah, the trouble paying attention? It’s definitely not a new thing, even if it feels a hundred times worse now that I'm stuck behind a desk all day. It’s always been there, just kind of humming in the background, making me lose my math homework.
